passage:
Salma arrived at the hospital canteen at the end of Zainab's night shift, carrying a steel tiffin and a face full of storm.
"Your Khala says you've accepted the Bengaluru transfer. Without asking us."
Zainab took the tiffin and set it down gently. "Ammi, sit. Yes, I accepted. It's my career, and I'm twenty-five. That decision is mine."
"And if we say no?"
"Then I'll be sad you said no. But I'm still going." She reached across and held her mother's hand. "I'll call every night. I'll come home for both Eids. You can visit and scold my cooking."
Salma's mouth trembled. "You'll forget us."
"Never. I'm not leaving you, Ammi. I'm only moving my work."
They sat quietly while the ward staff came in for tea. At last Salma opened the tiffin and pushed the parathas towards her. "Eat. You're too thin for Bengaluru."

qa.q: What did Salma bring to the hospital canteen?
qa.a: Salma brought a steel tiffin.

qa.q: What is Salma afraid of when she says "You'll forget us"?
qa.a: She fears losing her daughter's closeness and her own place in Zainab's life once Zainab moves away.

qa.q: Which part of Zainab's reply set a boundary while keeping affection?
qa.a: She calmly said the decision was hers and she was still going, while holding Ammi's hand and promising nightly calls and visits for both Eids.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel as her mother's mouth trembles?
qa.a: Zainab likely feels tender and a little sad, yet steady, holding her mother's hand and reassuring her, "I'm not leaving you, Ammi."

grounding: An adult daughter calmly keeps her decision to take a job transfer while holding her mother's hand and promising steady contact.

passage:
Dear Amma,
Leela Aunty from next door will have told you where I'm staying. I'm safe. The working women's hostel near my office is clean, and the warden is kind.
I didn't leave because I stopped loving you. I left because when I said no to the match, Papa broke the TV and said he would lock me in until I agreed. After that night I called a women's helpline, and they helped me find this place.
Here is what I can promise. I'll call you every Tuesday and Friday. I'll meet you at the temple on Sundays, if you want. I'll come home for the festival once Papa agrees, with someone else present, that there will be no threats.
What I won't do is let anyone else decide who I marry. That part is mine.
I miss your rasam. I miss you.
Your Shreya

qa.q: Where is Shreya staying now?
qa.a: Shreya is staying at the working women's hostel near the office.

qa.q: What does Shreya most want Amma to understand?
qa.a: Shreya wants Amma to know the love and missing are real, and that leaving was because of Papa's threats, not to cut Amma off.

qa.q: Which choice kept Shreya safe after that night?
qa.a: Calling a women's helpline, which helped find the hostel, gave Shreya safe housing and outside support before setting any terms with the family.

qa.q: What might Amma feel reading about the Tuesday and Friday calls?
qa.a: She may feel relief that Shreya hasn't cut contact, mixed with sadness and worry about what happened at home.

grounding: Shreya, who faced threats at home, gets outside help and safe housing, then keeps affection and contact with Amma on clear terms.

passage:
Gurleen, remember I told you I was dreading Sunday? I did it. I'm Himani, and I finally spoke to my parents.
They had been showing me photos of boys for a year. Every visit, another biodata. Papa said, "We know what's best." Mummy cried if I said no.
So on Sunday I sat them down, after lunch, calmly. I said, "I love you both. I'm not cutting you off. But I'll choose my own partner, and I'll decide when. Please stop sending biodatas."
Papa went silent. Mummy said, "After everything?" I stayed calm. I said, "I'll still come every Sunday. I'll still call Mummy every night. That doesn't change."
It wasn't magic. Papa didn't speak to me at dinner. But last night Mummy called, and asked about my day, not about boys.
If it had turned to threats or worse, I'd already saved a helpline number. Thank God it didn't.

qa.q: How long had Himani's parents been showing photos of boys?
qa.a: For a year.

qa.q: How did Himani feel while speaking to Mummy and Papa?
qa.a: Himani felt nervous but steady, staying calm and loving while holding firm about the choice.

qa.q: What made Himani's approach a good one?
qa.a: Himani spoke calmly, named what Himani alone would decide, kept up Sunday visits and nightly calls, and had a helpline ready in case of threats.

qa.q: How did Himani's parents react?
qa.a: Papa went silent and Mummy felt hurt at first, but later Mummy called and asked about Himani's day.

grounding: An adult child calmly tells parents about choosing a partner independently while keeping affection and contact, with help ready if threats arise.

passage:
I've lived next door to Jagdish Uncle and his son Asif for fifteen years, so I heard most of it through the open window on Sunday.
Asif had got a job offer in Hyderabad. His father wanted him to stay and join the family shop. Voices rose. Jagdish Uncle said, "If you go, don't come back asking for anything."
Then Asif spoke, and I remember how calm he sounded. "Abbu, I love you. I'm taking the job. I'll come home every month, and I'll call you every evening after the shop closes. I'm not leaving the family. I'm just choosing my work."
There was a long silence. I couldn't see their faces.
A month later, I saw Asif get out of an auto with a box of sweets and walk straight into the shop. His father didn't smile, exactly. But he took the box.
I don't know what either of them felt. But I know Asif kept coming.

qa.q: Where was Asif's job offer?
qa.a: In Hyderabad.

qa.q: How did Asif seem to feel when he answered his father?
qa.a: Asif seemed calm and loving, though probably nervous, firm about his decision while trying to keep the family close.

qa.q: What did Asif do that set a boundary without cutting off?
qa.a: He calmly said he would take the job, promised monthly visits and evening calls, and then kept coming home.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see the relationship a month later?
qa.a: The neighbour notices Asif returning with sweets and his father taking the box, though they can't know what either felt.

grounding: A neighbour observes an adult son calmly deciding his own career while keeping affection and contact with his father.

passage:
January. Yogesh told his father Santosh that he would marry Anjum, the woman he'd chosen. Santosh slammed his hand on the table, raised it toward him, and said, "Out of my house. Tonight." Yogesh's mother was crying in the kitchen doorway.
That same night, Yogesh went to his cousin's flat across town. He called a family counselling helpline from the balcony. They helped him think about staying safe and not going back alone while tempers were high.
February. He didn't cut his family off. He messaged his mother every evening. He told his father in a calm text, "I love you, Papa. I'm marrying Anjum. I'll visit when it's safe for all of us." No reply.
April. His mother met him at the temple. She held his hand for a long time. Then, in June, a short message came from Santosh: "Your mother misses you. Come for lunch Sunday. Bring her."
Yogesh read it three times before he could answer.

qa.q: Where did Yogesh go the night his father told him to leave?
qa.a: To his cousin's flat across town.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when he read his father's message in June?
qa.a: Yogesh felt overwhelmed and hopeful, reading it three times before he could answer.

qa.q: What steps did Yogesh take to stay safe and keep his boundary?
qa.a: He left that night for his cousin's flat, called a counselling helpline, stayed in contact by calm messages, and visited only when it was safe.

qa.q: How might Yogesh's mother have felt through these months?
qa.a: His mother was probably heartbroken and torn, crying at first, then meeting him at the temple and missing him.

grounding: It shows an adult son deciding his own marriage, seeking outside help and safe housing after a threat, while keeping affection and contact over months.

passage: You think I always got along with your Nana and Nani, Ishita? Not at all. When I was twenty-five, I got a teaching job in Shillong, and they wanted me to stay in Jaipur and marry the boy they had chosen. There was shouting. Your Nana said I'd be no daughter of his. I was frightened, but I didn't shout back. One evening I sat with them and said, "I love you. I'm taking the job. I'll decide who I marry. And I'll come home every Diwali." Then I did exactly that. The first Diwali, Nana barely spoke. The second, he asked about my students. By the fourth, he was sending me pickle. My friend Leela had it worse: her brothers threatened to lock her in, so she moved to a women's hostel with a counsellor's help. Different homes need different steps, beta. But calm words and kept promises, that is what worked for your Rekha maasi.

qa.q: Where did Rekha get a teaching job?
qa.a: In Shillong.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when Nana said she'd be no daughter of his?
qa.a: Rekha felt frightened, but stayed calm and chose not to shout back.

qa.q: Which choice in the story kept the relationship alive?
qa.a: Rekha said calmly what she would decide herself and kept her promise to come home every Diwali, so affection and contact continued.

qa.q: How did Nana's feelings seem to change over the Diwalis?
qa.a: Nana went from barely speaking, to asking about her students, to sending pickle, suggesting his anger softened as she kept coming back.

grounding: Shows an adult child calmly stating what she will decide and keeping contact with family, while a friend facing threats needed outside help and a safe hostel.
